BDK pp. 32–33

The two hindrances

Page 33 begins mid-sentence. The opening words from p. 32 complete the passage.

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

On the “defiled state of mind.” p. 32–33 It is called “the hindrance originating from defilements,” for it obstructs any fundamental insight into suchness.

On “ignorance.” Ignorance is called the “hindrance originating from misconceptions of objects,” for it obstructs the wisdom that functions spontaneously in the world.

Because of the defiled [state of] mind, there emerges the subject that perceives [incorrectly] ( i.e., the evolving mind) and that which reproduces [the reproducing mind], and thus one erroneously predicates the world of objects and causes oneself to deviate from the undifferentiated state [of suchness]. Though all things are always in quiescence and devoid of any marks of rising, because of the nonenlightenment due to ignorance, one erroneously strays from the Dharma (i.e., suchness); thus one fails to obtain the wisdom that functions spontaneously by adapting oneself to all circumstances in the world.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗
6. The two obstacles
BDK 32 ↗The two hindrances

The sixth part explains the two obstacles. In the explicit exposition they are called the “two hindrances.” In the implicit exposition they are called the “two obstacles.” I explain this at length in my Treatise on the Two Hindrances. The present passage follows the implicit exposition, in two parts.

  1. It first distinguishes the two obstacles. ↓

  2. From “what does this mean?” onward it explains the reasons for the distinction. ↓

6.1. Distinguishing the obstacles
The obstacle of the afflictions

↥ In the first part, “the defiled mind” refers to the six forms of defiled mind. “Fundamental wisdom” is the discernment that illuminates quiescence.ᵀ The defiled mind runs counter to quiescence and is therefore called the “obstacle of the afflictions.”

Fundamental wisdom · 根本智 gēn běn zhì · BDK p. 33 fundamental insight
The obstacle to wisdom
BDK 33 ↗On ignorance

“Ignorance” refers to root ignorance. “Wisdom that acts in the world” is subsequently acquired wisdom. Ignorance is so benighted that it can distinguish nothing. Hence it runs counter to the wisdom that makes distinctions in the world. This is the sense in which it is called the “obstacle to wisdom.”

6.2. Why each is an obstacle
BDK 33 ↗Because of the defiled state of mind

The explanation of the reasons makes this point explicit.

Defiled mind and fundamental wisdom

↥ “Because the defiled mind perceives, manifests, and delusively grasps objects” refers in brief to evolving consciousness, manifesting consciousness, and discriminating consciousness. † † “Runs counter to the nature of equality” means it runs counter to the equality of subject and object in fundamental wisdom.ᵀ This explains the obstacle of the afflictions.

evolving consciousness · 轉識 zhuǎn shí · BDK p. 27 evolving mind · pravṛttivijñāna (in the Laṅkāvatāra parallel) · The second mode is the stirred mind becoming the perceiver. Wŏnhyo also records wider uses of 轉識.

BDK 33 ↗Though all things are always in quiescence

“All dharmas are ever quiescent and exhibit no characteristic of arising” identifies the dharma-nature about which ignorance is deluded.ᵀ “Through ignorance and nonawakening one delusively runs counter to the Dharma” shows how ignorance is deluded about dharma-nature. † Hence the passage from “one cannot attain” through “[knowledge of every] kind” directly explains how ignorance runs counter to wisdom concerning the world.

3. The two hindrances
BDK 32–33 ↗The hindrance from defilements and the hindrance from misconceptions of objects

Beginning “further, the meaning of defiled mind,” the third section gathers these matters under two hindrances. There are, in brief, two ways of understanding them.

3.1. The account in other scriptures and treatises

↥ The first approach identifies an obstruction common to the two vehicles.⁕

  1. The afflictions of the ten latent tendencies keep one revolving in saṃsāra and obstruct the fruit of nirvāṇa. They are called the afflictive obstruction.

    1. Grasping at dharmas and similar delusions are a hindrance particular to bodhisattvas. They obscure what is to be known and obstruct the fruit of awakening. They are called the cognitive obstruction. This is the approach taught in other scriptures and treatises.

3.2. The account in the Awakening of Faith

↥ The second approach distinguishes the two as follows.

  1. Any mind that stirs in thought, grasps at characteristics, and so on runs counter to the quiescent nature of wisdom that knows reality as it is. This is called the afflictive hindrance.ᵀ

    afflictive hindrance · 煩惱礙 fán nǎo ài · BDK p. 32–33 hindrance originating from defilements

    1. Fundamental ignorance, dark, deluded, and unawakened, runs counter to the discerning activity of wisdom that knows phenomena in their full extent. This is called the hindrance to wisdom.ᵀ

      hindrance to wisdom · 智礙 zhì ài · BDK p. 33 hindrance originating from misconceptions of objects

↥ The present treatise adopts the second of these approaches.⁕ It therefore calls the six kinds of defiled mind the afflictive hindrance, and the underlying ground of ignorance the hindrance to wisdom. Yet if one matched them directly, one would expect ignorance to obstruct wisdom regarding reality, and defiled mind to obstruct wisdom regarding phenomena in their full extent. Why should it be otherwise? Because the match need not always hold. The treatise itself explains why it need not hold.

2. Subtle
BDK p. 34 ↗the other is “subtle,”

“Second, subtle, because it is unassociated with mind” refers to the following. † The last three defiled states of mind are unassociated. They lack the coarse, evident characteristic of a distinction between mind and mental factors. Their nature is subtle. They flow on without interruption. The sūtra calls this “the arising and ceasing of the continuum.”

unassociated · 不相應 bù xiāng yìng · BDK p. 34 disunited · viprayukta · Association here concerns the relation of mind to its distinguishable mental factors.
The two descriptions in the Laṅkāvatāra
BDK p. 34 ↗the other is “subtle,”

The ten-fascicle [Laṅkāvatāra] says, “Consciousness has two kinds of cessation. What are the two? First, cessation of characteristics. Second, cessation of the continuum. The same holds for arising and abiding.” The four-fascicle version says, “The consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing. There is the arising of the ongoing flow and the arising of characteristics. The same holds for cessation.” The sūtra simply gives the two names without specifying what characterizes each. The author of the treatise therefore uses association and nonassociation to distinguish what characterizes the coarse and the subtle.

2. The subtle
BDK p. 34 ↗for [those who belong to this category are] disunited from the [subtle activities of the…

“Second, the subtle, which is unassociated with mind.” The last three defilements are unassociated: † they lack the coarse differentiation into [mind and distinct] mental factors. Their very constitution is subtle. They flow on uninterruptedly, hence “arising and ceasing as a continuum.” The ten-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra says, “Consciousness ceases in two ways. What are the two? First, its manifest characteristics cease. Second, its continuity ceases. The same distinction applies to arising and persisting.” The four-fascicle version says, “The consciousnesses arise, persist, and cease in two ways. There is arising as a stream and arising in manifest characteristics. The same applies to persisting and ceasing.” The sūtra merely gives these two names. As it does not set out their distinguishing characteristics, the author of the treatise makes them explicit here.

p. 34 These two categories of beings in the phenomenal order come about because of the permeation of ignorance; that is to say, they come about because of the primary cause and the coordinating causes. Two causes for each kind of consciousness
BDK p. 34 ↗that is to say, they come about because of the primary cause and the coordinating causes.

In a full account each has two causes. ↓ ↓ The four-fascicle sūtra says, “Mahāmati, inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation are the causes of manifesting consciousness. Apprehending the various sense objects and the perfuming of beginningless deluded conception are the causes of the consciousness that discriminates objects.” †

consciousness that discriminates objects · 分別事識 fēn bié shì shí · BDK p. 36 object-discriminating consciousness · vastuprativikalpavijñāna (Laṅkāvatāra parallel)
Manifesting consciousness
BDK p. 34 ↗By the primary cause, “nonenlightenment” is meant;

To explain. “Inconceivable perfuming” means that ignorance can perfume suchness. It can perfume precisely where perfuming would seem impossible. This is why it is called inconceivable. “Inconceivable transformation” means that suchness undergoes the perfuming of ignorance. What cannot change nevertheless changes. This is why it is called “inconceivable transformation.” This perfuming and transformation are extremely subtle and hidden. Manifesting consciousness, which arises from them, is correspondingly subtle in its mode of activity. It also comprises evolving consciousness and activating consciousness. † The coarser is named and the subtler included with it. Hence [the sūtra] names only manifesting consciousness.

activating consciousness · 業識 yè shí · BDK p. 35 activating mind · *karmavijñāna (tentative) · In this treatise 業 names the initial activity of mind when stirred by ignorance.
Consciousness that discriminates objects
BDK p. 34 ↗and by the coordinating causes, “the erroneously represented world of objects.”

“Apprehending the various sense objects” refers to the various objects that manifesting consciousness apprehends. They can stir the ocean of mind and raise the waves of the seven consciousnesses.

BDK p. 34 ↗and by the coordinating causes, “the erroneously represented world of objects.”

In “the perfuming of beginningless deluded conception,” it is this very manifesting consciousness that is called deluded conception. From the outset it has never been free of conception. That is why this deluded conception is called beginningless. As the treatise said above, it is called “beginningless ignorance” because, from the outset, [mind] has never been free of thought. Understand “deluded conception” here in the same way. As the ten-fascicle sūtra says, “The cognition of ālayavijñāna is called the characteristic of consciousness. † Its nature and characteristics are like a ring of hairs appearing in empty space. They lie outside the domain of pure wisdom.” For this reason it is deluded conception. Those various sense objects and this deluded conception perfume the ocean of mind in its own characteristic, causing the waves of the seven consciousnesses to rise. Deluded conception and sense objects are coarse and evident. The consciousness that discriminates objects, which they give rise to, is therefore coarse and evident in its mode of activity. In this way it constitutes associated mind.

ālayavijñāna · 阿梨耶識 ā lí yé shí · BDK p. 16 storehouse consciousness · ālayavijñāna
Arising and persistence
BDK p. 34 ↗that is to say, they come about because of the primary cause and the coordinating causes.

The point is that manifesting consciousness comes to arise because of inconceivable perfuming and persists in dependence on inconceivable transformation. The consciousness that discriminates objects arises by taking the various sense objects as its conditions and persists in dependence on the perfuming of deluded conception. The treatise here takes up only the conditions for arising. Thus, for the subtle, it speaks only of the perfuming of ignorance. For the coarse, it names only objects as the condition.

2. What cessation means
BDK p. 34 ↗When the primary cause ceases to be, then the coordinating causes will cease to be.

The passage beginning “If the cause ceases” explains cessation next. It has two parts. The first sets out the meaning directly. ↓ The second, beginning with “Question,” uses an exchange to resolve doubts. ↓

1. Direct explanation
BDK p. 34 ↗When the primary cause ceases to be, then the coordinating causes will cease to be.

In the first part, “if the cause ceases, the condition ceases” means that at whatever stage the antidote is attained, ignorance as cause ceases, and objects cease accordingly.

BDK p. 34 ↗Because of the cessation of the primary cause, the mind disunited [from the represented…

“When the cause ceases, unassociated mind ceases.” The three kinds of unassociated mind arise in direct dependence on ignorance as cause. When ignorance ceases, they cease accordingly.

BDK p. 34 ↗and because of the cessation of the coordinating causes, the mind united [with the…

“When the condition ceases, associated mind ceases.” The three associated defiled states of mind arise in direct dependence on objects as their condition. When objects cease, these too cease accordingly. The two kinds of arising and ceasing are explained over their whole course, from first arising to final exhaustion. Arising and ceasing in each instant is a different issue.

Wŏnhyo · Separate NotesT1845 ↗

In explaining cessation, the text takes the more specific sense for the present. Thus “when the cause ceases, unassociated mind ceases,” and “when the condition [ceases], associated mind ceases.”

Two causes for each kind of consciousness
BDK p. 34 ↗that is to say, they come about because of the primary cause and the coordinating causes.

To give the full account, each of these two has two causes. As the four-fascicle sūtra says, “Mahāmati, inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation cause manifesting consciousness. ↓ Taking up various sense objects and the perfuming of beginningless delusive imagining cause the consciousness that discriminates objects.”⁕ † ↓

consciousness that discriminates objects · 分別事識 fēn bié shì shí · BDK p. 36 object-discriminating consciousness · vastuprativikalpavijñāna (Laṅkāvatāra parallel)
1. What gives rise to manifesting consciousness
BDK p. 34 ↗By the primary cause, “nonenlightenment” is meant;

“Inconceivable perfuming” refers to ignorance, since its power to perfume suchness is beyond measure. “Inconceivable transformation” refers to suchness receiving the perfuming of ignorance and changing although it cannot change.⁕ This perfuming and transformation are extremely subtle and hidden. The manifesting consciousness they give rise to thus operates subtly and is unassociated.

2. What gives rise to the consciousness that discriminates objects
BDK p. 34 ↗and by the coordinating causes, “the erroneously represented world of objects.”

“Beginningless delusive imagining” is this very manifesting consciousness, for it has never been free of imagining. As the text said above, “From the beginning it has never been free of thought. Hence we speak of beginningless ignorance.” So too with beginningless delusive imagining. “Various sense objects” are precisely the objects that manifesting consciousness presents. These two [imagining and its objects] perfume and stir the ālayavijñāna in its own characteristic, setting the seven consciousnesses in motion as waves. Because the imagining and its objects are coarse and evident, the seven consciousnesses they produce constitute associated mind. The present treatise singles out one factor in each case. For the subtle it speaks only of ignorance perfuming, and for the coarse it mentions only objects as the condition. It follows the progression from subtle to coarse to show what distinguishes their causes and conditions.

The general and specific accounts of cessation
BDK p. 34 ↗When the primary cause ceases to be, then the coordinating causes will cease to be.

Again, the four-fascicle sūtra says, “Mahāmati, when the many unreal fabrications that conceal true consciousness cease, all the consciousnesses of appearances cease. This is called the cessation of manifest characteristics.⁕ As for the cessation of continuity, when the cause of continuity ceases, continuity ceases. When what it depends on and what it takes as object cease, continuity ceases. Why? Because these are its causes. Its support is the perfuming of beginningless delusive imagining. Its objects are the delusively imagined objects of consciousness that appear from one’s own mind.” The sūtra speaks in this way because it takes the general approach. The treatise takes the specific sense, as explained above.

Four conditions for the arising of a consciousness
BDK p. 34 ↗that is to say, they come about because of the primary cause and the coordinating causes.

Speaking broadly of the causes and conditions of arising, each consciousness has four. As the ten-fascicle sūtra says, “There are four causes by which eye-consciousness arises. What four? First, one fails to recognize that what one takes as an object is within oneself. ↓ Second, one has been perfumed from beginningless time by falsely discriminating visible objects. ↓ Third, this is the very nature of consciousness itself. ↓ Fourth, one desires to see the various appearances of form.”⁕ ↓

BDK p. 34 ↗that is to say, they come about because of the primary cause and the coordinating causes.

The four-fascicle sūtra says, “Eye-consciousness becomes active owing to four conditions: failure to recognize that what one apprehends is one’s own mind made manifest, ↓ clinging under the influence of beginningless false impressions of forms experienced before, ↓ the nature proper to consciousness, ↓ and the desire to see various appearances of form. These are the four conditions. ↓ In that stream the storehouse consciousness stirs and the waves of consciousness arise.”

1. Fundamental ignorance
BDK p. 34 ↗By the primary cause, “nonenlightenment” is meant;

“Failure to recognize that what one apprehends is one’s own mind made manifest” identifies fundamental ignorance as a cause. The coarse appearance of form is presented by manifesting consciousness. It lies within the compass of one’s own mind, without existing outside consciousness. Hence “apprehending what one’s own mind manifests.”

BDK p. 34 ↗By the primary cause, “nonenlightenment” is meant;

“Failure to recognize” means that ignorance fails to recognize that visible objects have no external existence. It can therefore give rise to eye-consciousness and make it apprehend them as external. This is the first cause.

2. The perfuming of delusive imagining
BDK p. 34 ↗that is to say, they come about because of the primary cause and the coordinating causes.

The passage from “beginningless falsehood” through “clinging” identifies the perfuming of beginningless delusive imagining as a cause. Manifesting consciousness has always grasped at visible objects. These habitual impressions give rise to eye-consciousness and make it take up visible objects.

3. A preceding consciousness of the same kind
BDK p. 34 ↗that is to say, they come about because of the primary cause and the coordinating causes.

“The nature of consciousness” identifies a preceding member of the same kind as a cause. Earlier eye-consciousness discriminated by its very nature. Through that perfuming, eye-consciousness subsequently arises with the same nature as before.

4. The perfuming of verbal designations
BDK p. 34 ↗that is to say, they come about because of the primary cause and the coordinating causes.

“The desire to see various appearances of form” identifies perfuming by verbal designations as a cause. An earlier eye-consciousness sees an appearance of form. Mental consciousness takes that seeing eye-consciousness as its object, discriminates through mental speech, and clings to the desire to see. The other consciousnesses can be understood on the analogy of this account of the eye.

BDK p. 35

What ceases? Mind, wind, and water

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 35 Question: If the mind ceases to be, what will become of its continuity? If there is continuity of mind, how can you explain its final cessation?

p. 35 Answer: What we speak of as “cessation” is the cessation of the marks of [the deluded] mind only and not the cessation of its essence. It is like the case of the wind which, following the surface of the water, leaves the marks of its movement. If the water should cease to be, then the marks of the wind would be nullified and the wind would have no support [on which to display its movement]. But since the water does not cease to be, the marks of the wind may continue. Because only the wind ceases, the marks of its movement cease accordingly. This is not the cessation of water. So it is with ignorance; on the ground of the essence of Mind there is movement. If the essence of Mind were to cease, then people would be nullified and they would have no support. But since the essence does not cease to be, the mind may continue. Because only stupidity ceases to be, the marks of the [stupidity of the] mind cease accordingly. It is not that the wisdom (i.e., the essence) of Mind ceases.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

3. Characteristics of arising and ceasing

2. How the coarse and subtle arise and cease

3. Characteristics of arising and ceasing › 2. How the coarse and subtle arise and cease

2. What cessation means
2. Resolving doubts
1. The question
BDK p. 35 ↗Question: If the mind ceases to be, what will become of its continuity?

The second part uses an exchange to resolve doubts, first the question, then the answer. ↓ The question “If mind ceases, how can there be continuity?” addresses the teachings of non-Buddhists. As the ten-fascicle sūtra says, “If ālayavijñāna ceases, this is indistinguishable from the conceptual proliferation of the non-Buddhists’ annihilationist view. The non-Buddhists say, ‘When one is free of all objects, continuing consciousness ceases. Once continuing consciousness has ceased, all consciousnesses cease.’ Mahāmati, if continuing consciousness ceased, the consciousnesses [in operation] since beginningless time would have to cease.” The point is to spell out what the non-Buddhists maintain. When, for example, one is born in the heaven of nonperceiving beings or enters the attainment of nonperception, they say that one is free of all objects and continuing consciousness ceases. Since the root ceases, its branches cease along with it.

The Tathāgata’s reply in the sūtra
BDK p. 35 ↗Question: If the mind ceases to be, what will become of its continuity?

The Tathāgata refutes them as follows. Suppose that when beings enter nonperception their continuing consciousness, which is their root, ceases. The seeds of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses and the rest would cease with it, and the consciousnesses could not arise again upon emergence. Yet when beings emerge, their consciousnesses do arise again. One can therefore know that their continuing consciousness does not cease when they enter nonperception. This is the refutation.

How the treatise takes up the difficulty
BDK p. 35 ↗Question: If the mind ceases to be, what will become of its continuity?

On this basis the treatise poses its question. If the essence of mind ceased upon entering the attainment of nonperception or the attainment of cessation, † how could its continuity resume? Hence “if mind ceases, how can there be continuity?”

essence of mind · 心體 xīn tǐ · BDK p. 35 its essence
BDK p. 35 ↗If there is continuity of mind, how can you explain its final cessation?

If, upon entering those attainments, the essence of mind does not cease and the continuity resumes, how could this characteristic of continuity ever cease for good? Hence “how can one speak of final cessation?”

2. The answer
BDK p. 35 ↗Answer: What we speak of as “cessation” is the cessation of the marks of [the deluded]…

The answer has three parts: the teaching itself, an analogy, and its application. ↓ ↓ ↓

1. The teaching itself
BDK p. 35 ↗Answer: What we speak of as “cessation” is the cessation of the marks of [the deluded]…

In the teaching itself, “what we mean by cessation” refers, for example, to what is said of the consciousnesses upon entering nonperception and similar attainments. Only the characteristics of coarse consciousness cease. The essence of the ālaya mind persists. Hence “only the characteristics of mind cease.” The earlier statement that unassociated mind ceases with the cessation of its cause likewise refers only to the cessation of the characteristic of activation and the others within mind. It does not say that mind in its own characteristic, its essence, ceases.

2. The analogy
BDK p. 35 ↗It is like the case of the wind which, following the surface of the water, leaves the…

The analogy brings out the two senses of cessation separately. “As wind depends on water for the appearance of movement” illustrates how the wind of ignorance stirs in dependence on mind.

Continuity through meditative attainment
BDK p. 35 ↗But since the water does not cease to be, the marks of the wind may continue.

“If water ceased, the wind would be cut off and have nowhere to rest. Because the water persists, the characteristic of the wind continues.” This illustrates how, upon entry into nonperception and similar attainments, the essence of mind persists and the consciousnesses therefore continue. This answers the first question.

Final cessation
BDK p. 35 ↗Because only the wind ceases, the marks of its movement cease accordingly.

“When the wind alone ceases, the characteristic of movement ceases with it.” On reaching the stage of a buddha, ignorance ceases forever, † and with it cease all such movements as the characteristic of activation. Mind in its own characteristic, its essence, persists. Hence “the water itself does not cease.” This answers the second question, explaining final cessation.

characteristic of movement · 動相 dòng xiàng · BDK p. 35 marks of its movement
3. Applying the analogy
BDK p. 35 ↗It is not that the wisdom (i.e., the essence) of Mind ceases.

The application takes up the two preceding points in order. “The wisdom of mind does not cease.” Mind’s very capacity for subtle understanding is called its wisdom. † As the treatise says above, “the nature of wisdom remains intact.” This explains in what sense the mind’s own characteristic persists. The rest of the passage follows readily.

wisdom of mind · 心智 xīn zhì · BDK p. 35 wisdom (i.e., the essence) of Mind
Can mind in its own characteristic cease?
The difficulty
BDK p. 35 ↗and not the cessation of its essence.

Question. Is the own characteristic of this consciousness produced entirely by defiled conditions, or is there also a sense in which it does not derive from conditions? If it is produced entirely by defiled conditions, then when defiled dharmas are exhausted, its own characteristic ought to cease. † If its own characteristic persists because it does not derive from defiled conditions, it would exist of itself. Further, if saying its own characteristic ceases amounts to the view of annihilation, would saying its own characteristic persists amount in turn to the view of permanence?

defiled dharmas · 染法 rǎn fǎ · BDK p. 35 the defiled state
1. The account in terms of karmic maturation
BDK p. 35 ↗and not the cessation of its essence.

Answer. Some say the essence of the ālaya mind is a dharma of karmic maturation, produced solely by karma and the afflictions. Consequently, when karma and the afflictions are exhausted, the root consciousness is exhausted altogether. At buddhahood, however, there is also a pure consciousness associated with great perfect mirror wisdom, [brought about] by the two practices of merit and wisdom.⁕ What “mind” means is the same in both cases. It is in this sense that mind is said to reach buddhahood.

2. The account in terms of movement and stillness
BDK p. 35 ↗and not the cessation of its essence.

Others say that mind in its own characteristic is stirred in its entirety by ignorance. Ignorance moves what is still, making it stir. It does not bring something previously nonexistent into being. Thus it is the movement of this mind that arises because of ignorance. This is called the “characteristic of activation.” The mind that moves is originally mind. This too is called its own characteristic. In this respect it does not derive from ignorance. Yet this very mind that ignorance stirs also arises successively from preceding instances of its own kind. Thus one avoids the error of making it exist of itself, while allowing a sense in which it persists. When ignorance is exhausted, the characteristic of movement ceases with it. Through inceptive awakening, mind returns to its original source. †

inceptive awakening · 始覺 shǐ jué · BDK p. 18 the process of actualization of enlightenment
3. The assessment of the two accounts
BDK p. 35 ↗and not the cessation of its essence.

Still others say that both teachers have grounds for what they say, since both draw on statements in the sacred texts. The first teacher has grasped the intent of the Yogācārabhūmi, the second, the intent of the Awakening of Faith. Yet one cannot take the words literally as their meaning. Why? If one takes the first account literally, one is grasping at a self in dharmas. If one takes the second literally, one holds the view of a personal self. Further, clinging to the first entails annihilationism, and clinging to the second entails eternalism. Understand, then, that both meanings elude expression.

BDK p. 35 ↗and not the cessation of its essence.

Although they elude expression, they can also be expressed. For although it is not so, neither is it otherwise.

Wŏnhyo · Separate NotesT1845 ↗

2. How both kinds come to an end

2. How both kinds come to an end

2. What ceases and what continues

BDK p. 35 ↗Question: If the mind ceases to be, what will become of its continuity?

The exchange beginning “Question” further clarifies what ceases and what continues. “If the essence of mind ceased, sentient beings would be annihilated and would have no support.” † Here the ālayavijñāna in its own characteristic is called “the essence of mind,” and the other consciousnesses are spoken of as “sentient beings.” As the ten-fascicle sūtra says, “If the continuing consciousness ceased, the consciousnesses [that have persisted] since beginningless time would have to cease.”

essence of mind · 心體 xīn tǐ · BDK p. 35 its essence
BDK p. 35 ↗It is not that the wisdom (i.e., the essence) of Mind ceases.

“Because delusion alone ceases, the characteristic of mind ceases accordingly. Mind’s knowing does not cease.” † Only the characteristic of movement in mind ceases. The ceasing of that movement leaves the knowing of the unmoving mind intact.⁕ † This is precisely what it means for the characteristic of activity to cease while mind’s own characteristic continues.

characteristic of mind · 心相 xīn xiàng · BDK p. 35 marks of [the deluded] mind · lakṣaṇa (相)
characteristic of movement · 動相 dòng xiàng · BDK p. 35 marks of its movement
The question about consciousness in its own characteristic
BDK p. 35 ↗It is not that the wisdom (i.e., the essence) of Mind ceases.

Question. Does this consciousness in its own characteristic arise entirely from defiled conditions, or is there also a sense in which it does not derive from conditions? If it arises entirely from conditions, its own characteristic too will cease when defiled conditions are exhausted. But if, considered in its own characteristic, it takes shape independently of defiled conditions, that characteristic exists of itself.

1. The account in terms of maturation
BDK p. 35 ↗It is not that the wisdom (i.e., the essence) of Mind ceases.

Some say that the essence of mind comes about solely through karma and the afflictions, since it is a dharma of karmic maturation. When karma is exhausted, root consciousness comes completely to an end. Yet at buddhahood there is also a pure consciousness associated with mirror wisdom, produced by the two practices of merit and wisdom. What karma and afflictions produce differs from what merit and wisdom produce. The term “mind” has the same sense in both cases.⁕ This alone is the sense in which one says that mind reaches buddhahood.

2. The account in terms of movement and stillness
BDK p. 35 ↗It is not that the wisdom (i.e., the essence) of Mind ceases.

Others say that the essence of mind in its own characteristic is stirred up in its entirety by ignorance. What happens is that something still is set in motion. Nothing previously nonexistent is brought into existence. The movement of this mind depends on ignorance. It is called the characteristic of activity. The mind that moves is mind in its own right to begin with. This is called its own characteristic. Considered under that aspect, mind does not derive from ignorance. Yet the very mind moved by ignorance can also arise in succession from preceding instances of its own kind. This accounts for its continuing without entailing the error of existence from itself. When ignorance is exhausted, the characteristic of activity ceases, and mind, through inceptive awakening, returns to its original source. †

inceptive awakening · 始覺 shǐ jué · BDK p. 18 the process of actualization of enlightenment
Wŏnhyo’s assessment
BDK p. 35 ↗It is not that the wisdom (i.e., the essence) of Mind ceases.

Assessment. Both teachers have reason on their side, for both rely on what the sacred teachings say. How so? For the approach that sets its meaning out explicitly, the first account is sound. It captures the intent of the Yogācārabhūmi and related works. For the approach that keeps its meaning implicit, the second is sound. It captures the intent of this Awakening of Faith and related works. One must avoid fastening on either side alone or taking the wording for the meaning. Why? Taking the first account literally amounts to the view that dharmas have a self. Taking the second account in that way amounts to grasping at a personal self. Thus neither formulation ultimately admits of expression. Yet both can be expressed: although nothing can be settled as being so, neither can it be said that this is not so.

BDK pp. 35–36

Four kinds of perfuming

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 35 Because of the four kinds of permeation, the defiled state, and the pure state emerge and continue uninterrupted. They are 1) the pure state, which is called suchness; 2) the cause of all defilements, which is called ignorance; 3) the deluded mind, which is called the “activating mind”; 4) the erroneously conceived external world, which is called the “objects of the five senses and of the mind.”

p. 35 The meaning of permeation. Clothes in the world certainly have no scent in themselves but if man permeates them with perfumes, then they come to have a scent. It is just the same with the case we are speaking of. The pure state of suchness certainly has no defilement

p. 35–36 but if it is permeated by ignorance, then the marks of defilement appear on it.

p. 36 The defiled state of ignorance is indeed devoid of any purifying form but if it is permeated by suchness, then it will come to have a purifying influence.

2. A further explanation of how consciousness gives rise to dharmas

BDK p. 35 ↗Because of the four kinds of permeation,

With “Furthermore, because four dharmas perfume” we come to the following passage. The detailed explanation of the gateway of arising and ceasing has two parts. † The first, the detailed exposition proper, concluded above. Here begins the second, which takes up an earlier statement to clarify it further. What statement? The text said above that this consciousness has two aspects. It encompasses all dharmas and gives rise to all dharmas. The sense in which it encompasses them has already been explained in detail. The sense in which it gives rise to them still needs clarification. The text now sets it out fully.

gateway of arising and ceasing · 生滅門 shēng miè mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of phenomena
BDK p. 35 ↗Because of the four kinds of permeation,

The passage has five parts. ↓ The first announces the number of dharmas. The second lists them by name. The third explains perfuming in general. ↓ The fourth distinguishes the particular forms perfuming takes. ↓ The fifth explains which perfuming ends and which continues. ↓

1–2. The number and names of the dharmas

BDK p. 35 ↗They are 1) the pure state, which is called suchness;

The announcement of the number and the list of names are self-explanatory.

3. What perfuming means

BDK p. 35 ↗Clothes in the world certainly have no scent in themselves

The third part gives a simile and then applies it. ↓

The application of the simile
BDK p. 35 ↗The pure state of suchness certainly has no defilement

In the application, “the pure dharma of suchness” means original awakening. † † “The defiled dharma of ignorance” means nonawakening. These are two aspects of a single consciousness. Each perfumes the other, giving rise to the whole range of defiled and pure dharmas. This directly explains what the underlying sūtra calls inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation.

pure dharma · 淨法 jìng fǎ · BDK p. 35 the pure state
original awakening · 本覺 běn jué · BDK p. 17 original enlightenment
A question about the perfuming of suchness
BDK p. 35–36 ↗but if it is permeated by ignorance, then the marks of defilement appear on it.

Question. The Compendium of the Mahāyāna says that something can undergo perfuming only if it meets four conditions. It therefore says that a permanent dharma cannot undergo perfuming. Why does this text speak of perfuming suchness?

BDK p. 36 ↗but if it is permeated by suchness, then it will come to have a purifying influence.

Reply. There are two senses of perfuming. ↓ ↓ The Compendium is speaking specifically of perfuming that can be understood conceptually. For that reason it says that a permanent dharma does not undergo perfuming. This treatise explains inconceivable perfuming. Hence it says that ignorance perfumes suchness and suchness perfumes ignorance. The two works bring out different points, so their accounts are compatible.

BDK p. 35 ↗The pure state of suchness certainly has no defilement

Here in the gateway of arising and ceasing, the text calls original awakening, pure by nature, “suchness.” In that sense one can speak of perfuming. Here the reference is not to suchness within the gateway of suchness, † since that gateway does not speak of suchness as giving rise to anything.

gateway of suchness · 真如門 zhēn rú mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of the absolute

2. How perfuming gives rise to dharmas

BDK p. 35 ↗Because of the four kinds of permeation,

With “Furthermore, there are four kinds of perfuming,” the text continues its full explanation of the gateway of arising and ceasing. That explanation has two parts. The first, the direct exposition, has already been given. This second part takes up the earlier statement and clarifies it through perfuming. How so? The text said above that this consciousness has two aspects, that it encompasses all dharmas and gives rise to all dharmas. Its capacity to encompass them has already been explained at length. Its capacity to give rise to them still calls for clarification. Accordingly, the following passage explains at length how the two aspects of this consciousness perfume one another and thereby give rise to all defiled and pure dharmas. † There are three parts. The first treats defiled and pure perfuming together. ↓ The second, beginning with “How,” distinguishes the characteristics of the two kinds of perfuming. ↓ ↓ The third, beginning with “Furthermore,” considers the two together with respect to which comes to an end and which continues. ↓

pure dharmas · 淨法 jìng fǎ · BDK p. 35 the pure state

1. Defilement and purity considered together

BDK p. 35 ↗They are 1) the pure state, which is called suchness;

In the first part, “suchness” designates the aspect of original awakening, † and “ignorance” the aspect of nonawakening. It is precisely because one consciousness comprises these two aspects that they can perfume one another and give rise to everything. This directly explains what the source sūtra means by inconceivable perfuming and transformation. The remaining wording is clear.

original awakening · 本覺 běn jué · BDK p. 17 original enlightenment
Question about the perfuming of a permanent dharma
BDK p. 35–36 ↗but if it is permeated by ignorance, then the marks of defilement appear on it.

Question. The Compendium of the Mahāyāna says, “Something can receive perfuming only if it fulfills four requirements. Hence we say that a permanent dharma cannot receive perfuming.” Why, then, does the present text say that ignorance perfumes suchness? Answer. That treatise is speaking here of perfuming that can be conceived. On that account it says that a permanent dharma cannot receive perfuming. The present treatise speaks of inconceivable perfuming. On that account it says that ignorance perfumes suchness and suchness perfumes ignorance. Since perfuming has a different sense in the two cases, the two treatises are consistent.

BDK pp. 36–37

How defiled states arise

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda
a. Permeation of Ignorance

p. 36 How does the permeation [of ignorance] give rise to the defiled state and continue uninterrupted? It may be said that, on the ground of suchness (i.e., the original enlightenment], ignorance (i.e., nonenlightenment) appears.⁕ Ignorance, the primary cause of the defiled state, permeates into suchness.

p. 36 Because of this permeation a deluded mind results. Because of the deluded mind, [deluded thoughts further] permeate into ignorance. While the principle of suchness is yet to be realized, [the deluded mind], developing thoughts [fashioned in the state] of nonenlightenment, predicates erroneously conceived objects of the senses and of the mind. These erroneously conceived objects of the senses and of the mind, the coordinating causes in [bringing about] the defiled state, permeate into the deluded mind and cause the deluded mind to attach itself to its thoughts, to create various [evil] karma, and to undergo all kinds of physical and mental suffering.

p. 36 The permeation of the erroneously conceived objects of the senses and of the mind is of two kinds. One is the permeation that accelerates [deluded] thoughts, and the other is the permeation that accelerates attachments.

p. 36 The permeation of the deluded mind is of two kinds. One is the basic permeation by the “activating mind,” which causes arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas to undergo the suffering of samsara, and the other is the permeation that accelerates [the activities of] the “object-discriminating consciousness” and which makes ordinary people suffer from the bondage of their karma.

p. 37 The permeations of ignorance are of two kinds. One is the basic permeation, since it can put into operation the “activating mind,” and the other is the permeation that develops perverse views and attachments, since it can put in operation the “object-discriminating consciousness.”

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. A further explanation of how consciousness gives rise to dharmas

2. A further explanation of how consciousness gives rise to dharmas

4. The particular forms of perfuming

BDK p. 36 ↗How does the permeation [of ignorance] give rise to the defiled state and continue…

The question “How?” opens the fourth part, which treats the particular forms of perfuming. It has two parts, first defilement, then purity. ↓ ↓

1. How defiled dharmas arise
BDK p. 36 ↗How does the permeation [of ignorance] give rise to the defiled state and continue…

The discussion of defilement consists of a question and an answer. The answer first explains briefly and then gives a detailed exposition. ↓ ↓

The answer in brief
What perfumes and what undergoes perfuming
BDK p. 36 ↗It may be said that, on the ground of suchness (i.e., the original enlightenment],…

In the brief explanation, “ignorance exists in dependence on the dharma of suchness” identifies what does the perfuming and what undergoes it. “Because there is ignorance, it perfumes suchness” describes perfuming by fundamental ignorance. “Because of perfuming, there is deluded mind” means that perfuming by ignorance gives rise to mind as activating consciousness.

How the process develops
BDK p. 36 ↗Because of the deluded mind, [deluded thoughts further] permeate into ignorance.

This deluded mind in turn perfumes ignorance, intensifying its failure to understand. Thus evolving consciousness and manifesting consciousness, among others, take shape. Hence the words “in nonawakening a thought arises and a delusive field of objects appears.” This field of objects in turn perfumes manifesting consciousness, hence “perfumes deluded mind.” “Makes it think of and cling to them” means that the seventh consciousness arises. “Creates various kinds of karma” means that mental consciousness arises. “Undergoes all suffering” means experiencing the results of that karma.

The answer in detail
BDK p. 36 ↗The permeation of the erroneously conceived objects of the senses and of the mind is of…

The detailed account expands on three points made above. It takes them in reverse order and begins with the field of objects. ↓

1. Perfuming by the field of objects
BDK p. 36 ↗One is the permeation that accelerates [deluded] thoughts,

“Intensifies thought.” The power of objects † strengthens the discriminative thought that grasps at dharmas in the consciousness that discriminates objects. “Intensifies clinging” means strengthening the four kinds of clinging that constitute an afflictive obstruction.

Intensifies thought · 增長念 zēng zhǎng niàn · BDK p. 36 accelerates [deluded] thoughts
2. Perfuming by deluded mind
1. Fundamental perfuming by activating consciousness
BDK p. 36 ↗One is the basic permeation by the “activating mind,”

Under perfuming by deluded mind, “fundamental perfuming by activating consciousness” † means that activating consciousness can perfume ignorance. In its delusion regarding the absence of characteristics, it can give rise to the ongoing succession of the characteristics of evolving and manifesting.

fundamental perfuming · 根本熏習 gēn běn xūn xí · BDK p. 36 basic permeation
BDK p. 36 ↗which causes arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas to undergo the suffering of samsara,

When followers of the three vehicles leave the three realms, they escape the coarse suffering of successive lifetimes associated with the consciousness that discriminates objects. They still undergo transformational birth and death in the ālaya, with the suffering inherent in conditioned formations. Hence the text speaks of the suffering of arising and ceasing experienced by followers of the three vehicles. † Generally speaking, this suffering has existed without beginning. The text wants to distinguish the coarse and subtle kinds of perfuming, so it speaks specifically of the time after coarse suffering has been left behind.

suffering of arising and ceasing · 生滅苦 shēng miè kǔ · BDK p. 36 suffering of samsara
2. Intensification of object discrimination
BDK p. 36 ↗and the other is the permeation that accelerates [the activities of] the…

“Perfuming that intensifies the consciousness that discriminates objects” refers to the suffering of successive lifetimes at the stage of an ordinary being.

3. Perfuming by ignorance
BDK p. 37 ↗The permeations of ignorance are of two kinds.

Under perfuming by ignorance, “fundamental perfuming” means fundamental nonawakening. “Perfuming by the views and craving to which it gives rise” refers to the views and craving in mental consciousness that arise from ignorance. † This is derivative nonawakening, the branches and tips.

1. How defilement arises
1. Brief account
BDK p. 36 ↗Because of this permeation a deluded mind results.

The second part, which distinguishes the two kinds, begins by explaining how defilement arises. It first gives a brief account and then explains in detail. ↓ “Through perfuming there is a deluded mind” refers to activating consciousness. † This deluded mind in turn perfumes ignorance, perpetuating ignorance of the absence of characteristics. Hence the deluded mind comes to have a perceiving aspect and manifests the characteristics of objects.

activating consciousness · 業識 yè shí · BDK p. 35 activating mind · *karmavijñāna (tentative) · In this treatise 業 names the initial activity of mind when stirred by ignorance.
BDK p. 36 ↗[the deluded mind], developing thoughts [fashioned in the state] of nonenlightenment,…

The text says, “In nonawakening a thought arises, manifesting delusive objects.” † “In nonawakening a thought arises” is the characteristic of evolving; the “delusive objects” are the characteristic of manifesting. These objects perfume the deluded mind just mentioned, raising the waves of the seven consciousnesses, which cling to the objects before them. Hence the text says that the objects “then perfume the deluded mind and bring about its thinking and attachment,” and so forth.⁕ † This concludes the brief account. A detailed explanation follows.

1. Perfuming by objects
1. Increasing thought
BDK p. 36 ↗One is the permeation that accelerates [deluded] thoughts,

“Increasing thought” means discrimination that takes dharmas to be real in themselves. †

2. Increasing clinging

2. Perfuming by deluded mind
1. Fundamental perfuming
BDK p. 36 ↗One is the basic permeation by the “activating mind,”

As for “fundamental perfuming by activating consciousness,” † this consciousness perfumes ignorance. Through delusion about the absence of characteristics, the perceiving aspect and the appearance of objects arise. Perceiving and appearances continue, and birth and death go on without interruption. This perceiving and these appearances occur within ālayavijñāna. † Practitioners of the three vehicles have escaped the coarse suffering of successive, finite lives bound by karma, which belongs to consciousness that discriminates objects. They still experience the subtle stress of fabrications in ālayavijñāna. Hence the text speaks of the suffering of arising and ceasing experienced by those of the three vehicles. †

2. Strengthening discrimination
BDK p. 36 ↗and the other is the permeation that accelerates [the activities of] the…

As for “perfuming that strengthens consciousness that discriminates objects,” mental consciousness gains strength from the afflictions of views and craving. † This allows it to experience the fruit of karma that binds one to the three realms. Hence the text speaks of ordinary beings’ suffering under karmic bondage. † †

3. Perfuming by ignorance
1. Fundamental perfuming
BDK p. 37 ↗One is the basic permeation, since it can put into operation the “activating mind,”

Under perfuming by ignorance, “fundamental perfuming” means that fundamental ignorance perfumes suchness, setting thought in motion. This is called activating consciousness. Hence the words “bringing activating consciousness into being.”

2. Perfuming by views and craving
BDK p. 37 ↗and the other is the permeation that develops perverse views and attachments,

As for “perfuming by the views and craving that [ignorance] gives rise to,” the views and craving that arise from fundamental ignorance perfume mental consciousness and give rise to coarse discrimination. This is called consciousness that discriminates objects. As the text said above, mental consciousness is here called consciousness that discriminates objects because the afflictions of views and craving strengthen it. Hence the words “bringing consciousness that discriminates objects into being.”

BDK pp. 37–38

How pure states arise

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda
b. Permeation of Suchness

p. 37 How does the permeation [of suchness] give rise to the pure state and continue uninterrupted? It may be said that there is the principle of suchness, and it can permeate into ignorance. Through the force of this permeation, [suchness causes the deluded mind to loathe the suffering of samsara⁕ and to aspire for nirvana. Because this mind, though still deluded, is [now] possessed with loathing and aspiration, permeates into suchness [in that it induces suchness to manifest itself]. Thus a person comes to believe in his essential nature, to know that what exists is the erroneous activity of the mind and that the world of objects in front of him is non existent, and to practice teachings to free himself [from the erroneously conceived world of objects]. He knows what is really so—that there is no world of objects in front of him— and therefore with various devices he practices courses by which to conform [himself to suchness]. He will not attach himself to anything nor give rise to any [deluded] thoughts. Through the force of this permeation [of suchness] over a long period of time, his ignorance ceases. Because of the cessation of ignorance, there will be no more rising of the [deluded activities of ] mind.

p. 37–38 Because of the nonarising [of the deluded activities of mind],

p. 38 the world of objects [as previously conceived] ceases to be; because of the cessation of both the primary cause (ignorance) and the coordinating cause (objects), the marks of the [defiled] mind will all be nullified. This is called “gaining nirvana and accomplishing spontaneous acts.”

p. 38 The permeation [of suchness] into the deluded mind is of two kinds.⁕ The first is the permeation into the “object-discriminating consciousness.” [Because of this permeation], ordinary people and the Hinayanists come to loathe the suffering of samsara, and thereupon each, according to his capacity, gradually advances toward the highest enlightenment (Ch., dao). The second is the permeation into mind. [Because of this permeation,] bodhisattvas advance to nirvana rapidly and with aspiration and fortitude.

p. 38 Two kinds of permeation of suchness [into ignorance] can be identified. The first is “the permeation through manifestation of the essence [of suchness],⁕ and the second is “the permeation through [external] influences.”

2. A further explanation of how consciousness gives rise to dharmas › 4. The particular forms of perfuming

2. How pure dharmas arise
BDK p. 37 ↗How does the permeation [of suchness] give rise to the pure state and continue uninterrupted?

The next “How?” introduces perfuming that gives rise to purity. A question is followed by an answer. The answer also has a brief explanation and a detailed exposition. ↓ ↓

The answer in brief
BDK p. 37 ↗and it can permeate into ignorance.

The brief account first explains “perfuming by suchness,” then “perfuming by deluded mind.” The latter has five steps. ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓

1. Faith at the ten stages of faith
BDK p. 37 ↗Thus a person comes to believe in his essential nature,

First, the passage from “because this deluded mind” through “has faith in its own nature” describes faith at the stage of the ten faiths.

2. Practice at the three stages of the worthy
BDK p. 37 ↗and to practice teachings to free himself [from the erroneously conceived world of objects].

Next, “knows that mind moves delusively and that no objects stand before it, and practices the dharma of disengagement” describes practice in the three groups of stages of the worthy.

3. The path of seeing
BDK p. 37 ↗He knows what is really so—that there is no world of objects in front of him—

“Because one knows in accordance with reality that no objects stand before one” shows that contemplation of consciousness-only comes to fruition on the path of seeing at the first ground.

4. The path of cultivation
BDK p. 37 ↗and therefore with various devices he practices courses by which to conform [himself to…

The words from “various” through “owing to the power of perfuming over a long time” describe cultivating the myriad practices on the path of cultivation through the ten grounds.

5. The fruit
BDK p. 37 ↗his ignorance ceases.

Fifth, from “ignorance then ceases,” the text describes realizing nirvāṇa at the stage of fruition.

The answer in detail
1. Perfuming by deluded mind
1. Consciousness that discriminates objects
BDK p. 38 ↗The first is the permeation into the “object-discriminating consciousness.”

The detailed exposition begins with perfuming by deluded mind. Here, in a broad sense, all seven consciousnesses can be called “consciousness that discriminates objects.” If one singles out the consciousness in which this function predominates, only mental consciousness is meant. Its discriminating activity is strong, and it takes all particular things as its objects. The present passage uses the term in that narrower sense. This consciousness does not know that sense objects are consciousness-only and therefore grasps at a field of objects as really existing outside mind. Ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles make progress toward the goal, † yet still conceive of saṃsāra as something to recoil from and nirvāṇa as something to desire. Their grasping remains that of the consciousness that discriminates objects. For this reason the text calls it “perfuming by the consciousness that discriminates objects.”

two vehicles · 二乘 èr shèng · BDK p. 42 the Hinayanists · śrāvakayāna and pratyekabuddhayāna · The two vehicles are those of disciples and solitary buddhas.
2. Perfuming by mentation
BDK p. 38 ↗The second is the permeation into mind.

“Perfuming by mentation (manas)” is also called “perfuming by activating consciousness.” † Broadly speaking, all five modes of consciousness are called mentation, as explained above. If one singles out their basis, only activating consciousness is meant. It is the subtlest of them and forms the basis of the other consciousnesses. That is why activating consciousness is here called mentation.

Perfuming by mentation · 意熏習 yì xūn xí · BDK p. 38 permeation into mind · manas (意) · Wŏnhyo interprets 意 here through 業識, the subtlest mode of mind.
BDK p. 38 ↗The second is the permeation into mind.

Within this activating consciousness, the perceiving side and the appearing object have yet to differentiate. Bodhisattvas know that mind stirs delusively and that there is no field of objects apart from it. They understand that all dharmas amount to consciousness alone. They abandon their previous grasping at external things and accord with activating consciousness in this respect. This is why the text calls it “perfuming by activating consciousness,” or “perfuming by mentation.” It does not mean that activating consciousness as produced by ignorance can itself arouse the aspiration for awakening and undertake the practices.

2. Perfuming by suchness
BDK p. 38 ↗Two kinds of permeation of suchness [into ignorance] can be identified.

The account of perfuming by suchness has three parts. It first announces the number of kinds, then lists their names, and finally distinguishes their characteristics. In distinguishing the characteristics, the text first explains the two kinds separately and then treats them together. ↓ ↓

2. How purity arises
BDK p. 37 ↗How does the permeation [of suchness] give rise to the pure state and continue uninterrupted?

The account of how pure dharmas arise likewise begins with a brief explanation and proceeds to a detailed one. ↓ The brief explanation is clear.

The two ways deluded mind perfumes
1. Consciousness that discriminates objects
BDK p. 38 ↗The first is the permeation into the “object-discriminating consciousness.”

In the detailed explanation, consider “perfuming by consciousness that discriminates objects.” In a broad sense, all seven consciousnesses are called consciousness that discriminates objects, as explained above. Taking the predominant case, the expression designates mental consciousness alone, since its power of discrimination is strong and it takes every sort of particular thing as its object. The passage here uses the term in this narrower sense. This consciousness fails to recognize that the sense objects are manifestations of evolving consciousness, † and takes objects outside the mind to be real. Ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles do turn toward the path, † yet they conceive of saṃsāra as something to recoil from and nirvāṇa as something to welcome. This preserves their initial way of grasping. Hence the name “perfuming by consciousness that discriminates objects.”

evolving consciousness · 轉識 zhuǎn shí · BDK p. 27 evolving mind · pravṛttivijñāna (in the Laṅkāvatāra parallel) · The second mode is the stirred mind becoming the perceiver. Wŏnhyo also records wider uses of 轉識.
two vehicles · 二乘 èr shèng · BDK p. 42 the Hinayanists · śrāvakayāna and pratyekabuddhayāna · The two vehicles are those of disciples and solitary buddhas.
2. Mentation
BDK p. 38 ↗The second is the permeation into mind.

As for “perfuming by mentation,” † in the broad sense all five modes of consciousness described above are called mentation, as explained earlier. When the reference is to their root, activating consciousness alone is called mentation, since it is the subtlest consciousness and serves as the basis of the others. What does “activating consciousness” mean? Although thought stirs, perceiving and what appears have yet to be distinguished. There is only what is present as consciousness. This is activating consciousness.

perfuming by mentation · 意熏習 yì xūn xí · BDK p. 38 permeation into mind · manas (意) · Wŏnhyo interprets 意 here through 業識, the subtlest mode of mind.
BDK p. 38 ↗The second is the permeation into mind.

As for these bodhisattvas, [they understand that] mind stirs in delusion and there are no objects apart from it,⁕ that all other dharmas are only what is present as consciousness. [They relinquish] all their former coarse attachments. In this their understanding resembles the characteristic of activating consciousness. Hence the name “perfuming by activating consciousness” or “perfuming by mentation.” This is no claim that the activating consciousness arising from ignorance can itself realize the principle of consciousness-only.

BDK pp. 38–40

Perfuming through suchness itself

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 38 (1) Permeation through Manifestation of the Essence of Suchness. [The essence of suchness] is, from the beginningless beginning,

p. 39 endowed with the “perfect state of purity.” It is provided with suprarational functions and the nature of manifesting itself.⁕ Because of these two reasons it permeates perpetually [into ignorance]. Through the force of [this permeation] it induces a person to loathe the suffering of samsara, to seek bliss in nirvana, and, believing that he has the principle of suchness within himself, to make up his mind to exert himself.

p. 39 Question: If this is so, then all sentient beings are endowed with suchness and are equally permeated by it. Why is it that there are infinite varieties of believers and nonbelievers, and that there are some who believe sooner and some later? All of them should, knowing that they are endowed with the principle of suchness, at once make an effort utilizing expedient means and should all equally attain nirvana.

p. 39 Answer: Though suchness is originally one, yet there are immeasurable and infinite [shades of] ignorance. From the very beginning ignorance is, because of its nature, characterized by diversity, and its degree of intensity is not uniform.

p. 39–40 Defilements, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges [River],

p. 40 come into being because of [the differences in intensity of] ignorance, and exist in manifold ways; defilements, such as the belief in the existence of atman and the indulgence in passion, develop because of ignorance and exist in different ways. All these defilements are brought about by ignorance, in an infinitely diversified manner in time. The Tathāgatas alone know all about this.

p. 40 In Buddhism there is [a teaching concerning] the primary cause and the coordinating causes. When the primary cause and the coordinating causes are sufficiently provided, there will be the perfection [of a result]. It is like the case of wood: though it possesses a [latent] fire nature which is the primary cause of its burning, it cannot be made to burn by itself unless people understand the situation and resort to means [of actualizing fire out of wood by kindling it]. In the same way a human being, though he is in possession of the correct primary cause, [suchness with] permeating force, cannot put an end to his defilements by himself alone and enter nirvana unless he is provided with coordinating causes, i.e., his encounters with the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, or good spiritual friends. Even though coordinating causes from without may be sufficiently provided, if the pure principle (i.e., suchness) within is lacking in the force of permeation, then a person cannot ultimately loathe the suffering of samsara and seek bliss in nirvana.

p. 40 However, if both the primary and the coordinating causes are sufficiently provided, then because of his possession of the force of permeation [of suchness from within] and the compassionate protection of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas [from without], he is able to develop a loathing for suffering, to believe that nirvana is real, and to cultivate his capacity for goodness. And when his cultivation of the capacity for goodness matures, he will as a result meet the Buddhas and bodhisattvas and will be instructed, taught, benefited, and given joy, and then he will be able to advance on the path to nirvana.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. Resolving the doubt
BDK p. 39 ↗Why is it that there are infinite varieties of believers and nonbelievers, and that there…

From “Question,” a question and answer resolve the doubt. The intent of the question is clear. The answer has two parts. The first explains unequal attainment in terms of the greater or lesser strength of afflictions. ↓ The second explains it in terms of differences in the conditions one encounters. ↓

1. Differences in affliction
BDK p. 39–40 ↗Defilements, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges [River],

In the first part, “higher afflictions more numerous than the sands of the Ganges” † means being confused about the various Dharma teachings and ignorant about particular things. This falls under the cognitive obstruction. “The afflictions of self-view and the defilement of craving” fall under the afflictive obstruction. † The intent of the answer is clear.

2. Differences in the conditions encountered
BDK p. 40 ↗In Buddhism there is [a teaching concerning] the primary cause and the coordinating causes.

The passage beginning “Furthermore, in the Dharma of the buddhas” explains the diversity of conditions. Its statement, simile, and application are evident in the text.

The Separate Notes pass directly from the two modes of deluded mind to the external conditions. Their commentary resumes with particular conditions (pp. 40–42).

BDK pp. 40–42

Particular conditions for awakening

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 40 (2) Permeation through Influences. This is the force from without affecting human beings by providing coordinating causes.

p. 40–41 Such external coordinating causes have an infinite number of meanings.

p. 41 Briefly, they may be explained under two categories: namely, the specific and the general coordinating causes.

p. 41 (a) The Specific Coordinating Causes. A person, from the time when he first aspires to seek enlightenment until he becomes an Enlightened One, sees or meditates on the Buddhas and bodhisattvas [as they manifest themselves to him]; sometimes they appear as his family members, parents, or relatives, sometimes as servants, sometimes as close friends, or sometimes as enemies. Through all kinds of deeds and incalculable performances, such as the practice of the four acts of loving-kindness, etc., they exercise the force of permeation created by their great compassion, and are thus able to cause sentient beings to strengthen their capacity for goodness and are able to benefit them as they see or hear [about their needs].

p. 41 This [specific] coordinating cause is of two kinds. One is immediate and enables a person to obtain deliverance quickly; and the other is remote and enables a person to obtain deliverance after a long time. The immediate and remote causes are again of two kinds: the causes which strengthen a person in his practices [of expedient means to help others], and those which enable him to obtain enlightenment (Ch., dao).

2. Equal conditions
BDK p. 42 ↗(b) The General Coordinating Causes.

The “equal conditions” † serve as conditions for perfuming by activating consciousness in bodhisattvas. Who can supply these conditions? Only “dharmakāya bodhisattvas” and those beyond them can do so, † since this requires “the power of wisdom that knows a shared essence.” † Thus [the vision] is attained “in dependence on samādhi.” †

equal conditions · 平等緣 píng děng yuán · BDK p. 42 General Coordinating Causes · pratyaya (緣)
dharmakāya bodhisattvas · 法身菩薩 fǎ shēn pú sà · BDK p. 43 bodhisattvas who realize the dharmakāya · dharmakāya (法身)
power of wisdom that knows a shared essence · 同體智力 tóng tǐ zhì lì · BDK p. 42 power of the wisdom that is one [with suchness]
samādhi · 三昧 sān mèi · BDK p. 42 concentration · samādhi
BDK p. 42 ↗[Because of this indiscriminately permeating cause], human beings are all equally able, by…

As for “seeing the buddhas equally,” bodhisattvas from the ten understandings [the ten abodes] onward all see the buddhas’ recompense bodies through activating consciousness. Their immeasurable major and minor characteristics are all boundless, free of any characteristic that would mark out a limit. Hence “seeing equally.” For a coarse, distracted mind to see such inconceivable characteristics would be impossible. Hence “only in dependence on samādhi does one see.”

BDK pp. 42–43

Before and after union with suchness

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 42 This permeation through the influence of the wisdom whose essence is one [with suchness] is also divided into two categories [according to the types of recipients].⁕

p. 42 The one is yet to be united [with suchness]. Ordinary people, the Hinayanists, and those bodhisattvas who have just been initiated devote themselves to religious practices on the strength of their faith, being permeated by suchness through their mind and consciousness.⁕

p. 42–43 Not having obtained the indiscriminate mind, however, they are yet to be united with the essence [of suchness],

p. 43 and not having obtained [the perfection of] the discipline of free acts, they are yet to be united with the influence [of suchness].

p. 43 The other is the already united [with suchness]: bodhisattvas who realize the dharmakāya have obtained undiscriminating mind [and are united with the essence of the Buddhas; they, having obtained free acts,]⁕ are united with the influence of the wisdom of the Buddhas. They singly devote themselves with spontaneity to their religious disciplines, on the strength of suchness within; permeating into suchness [so that suchness will reclaim itself], they destroy ignorance.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. Essence and activity considered together
BDK p. 42 ↗This permeation through the influence of the wisdom whose essence is one [with suchness]…

The separate explanations of perfuming by essence and by activity conclude here. † The second part explains essence and activity together. It begins with a general statement and then treats each case separately. ↓

perfuming by essence and by activity · 體用熏習 tǐ yòng xūn xí · BDK p. 42 permeation through the influence of the wisdom whose essence is one [with suchness] · Wŏnhyo construes 體用 as two aspects, essence and activity.
1. Those who have yet to accord
BDK p. 42 ↗being permeated by suchness through their mind and consciousness.

The separate explanation begins with those who have yet to accord. On the words “perfuming by mentation and mental consciousness”: in ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles, this is called perfuming by mental consciousness. It is perfuming by the consciousness that discriminates objects. In “bodhisattvas who have just aroused the aspiration,” from the ten understandings [the ten abodes] onward, it is called perfuming by mentation. † This means perfuming by activating consciousness, as explained earlier.

bodhisattvas who have just aroused the aspiration · 初發意菩薩 chū fā yì pú sà · BDK p. 42 bodhisattvas who have just been initiated
BDK p. 42–43 ↗Not having obtained the indiscriminate mind, however, they are yet to be united with the…

They “have yet to attain the nondiscriminating mind that accords with the essence,” † since they have yet to accord with the essence of the buddhas’ dharmakāya. and “have yet to attain unimpeded activity that accords with [the buddhas’] activity,” since they have yet to accord with the activity of the buddhas’ responsive and transformation bodies.

nondiscriminating mind · 無分別心 wú fēn bié xīn · BDK p. 42–43 indiscriminate mind
2. Those who already accord
BDK p. 43 ↗bodhisattvas who realize the dharmakāya have obtained undiscriminating mind [and are…

Among those who already accord, “dharmakāya bodhisattvas” are bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. † † They “attain nondiscriminating mind” because they accord with the essence. They “accord with the activity of the buddhas’ wisdom” because they possess wisdom that knows things in their full diversity. † They “practice spontaneously” because from the eighth ground onward practice proceeds without deliberate effort. †

2. How purity arises
Association with essence and activity

2. How perfuming gives rise to dharmas › 2. The two kinds of perfuming distinguished › 2. How purity arises › Association with essence and activity

1. Those not yet associated
BDK p. 42 ↗being permeated by suchness through their mind and consciousness.

In the account of those not yet associated, the text speaks of “perfuming by mentation and mental consciousness.” † Bodhisattvas rely on the perfuming of activating consciousness, here called “mentation.” The consciousness that discriminates objects in ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles is called “mental consciousness.” Here the comparison is with dharmakāya bodhisattvas at the time they realize the dharmakāya. At that time they are free of the characteristic of a perceiver. Accordingly, it is the bodhisattvas before the [ten] grounds for whom the text speaks of “perfuming by mentation,” since they rely on activating consciousness and retain the characteristic of a perceiver. If we consider seeing the recompense buddha by conventional wisdom, all stages up to and including the adamantine stage retain the characteristic of perceiving. Broadly speaking, all fall under “perfuming by activating consciousness.” This is explained below.

not yet associated · 未相應 wèi xiāng yìng · BDK p. 42 yet to be united
BDK p. 43

Which kinds of perfuming come to an end?

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 43 Again, the defiled principle (dharma), from the beginningless beginning, continues perpetually to permeate until it perishes by the attainment of Buddhahood. But the permeation of the pure principle has no interruption and no ending. The reason is that the principle of suchness is always permeating; therefore, when the deluded mind ceases to be, the dharmakāya (i.e., suchness, original enlightenment) will be manifested and will give rise to the permeation of the influence [of suchness], and thus there will be no ending to it.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. A further explanation of how consciousness gives rise to dharmas

2. A further explanation of how consciousness gives rise to dharmas

5. Which perfuming ends and which continues

BDK p. 43 ↗Again, the defiled principle (dharma), from the beginningless beginning, continues…

Of the five parts of this further explanation based on an earlier statement, the fourth, distinguishing the two kinds of perfuming, is now complete. The fifth explains which of the two kinds ends and which continues. Defiled perfuming arises in opposition to reality and therefore comes to an end. Perfuming by pure dharmas arises in accord with reality. Since it accords with reality, it never comes to an end. The wording is clear.

Wŏnhyo · Separate NotesT1845 ↗

The greatness of the essence of suchness

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda
II. The Essence Itself and the Attributes of Suchness, or the Meanings of Mahā · A. The Greatness of the Essence of Suchness

p. 44 [The essence of suchness] knows no increase or decrease in ordinary people, the Hinayanists, the bodhisattvas, or the Buddhas. It was not brought into existence in the beginning nor will it cease to be at the end of time; it is eternal through and through.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. The meaning of “Great Vehicle”

BDK p. 44 ↗[The essence of suchness] knows no increase or decrease in ordinary people, the…

The exposition proper in “Revealing the correct meaning” has two main parts. The first, explaining the heading “dharma,” has concluded. This second part explains the heading “meaning.” The earlier section establishing the meaning set out two meanings: the meaning of “great” and that of “vehicle.” The present passage directly explains “great,” while also bringing out the sense of “vehicle.” It has two parts. The first treats greatness in essence and greatness in characteristics together. ↓ The second separately explains greatness in activity.

1. The greatness of essence and characteristics

BDK p. 44 ↗[The essence of suchness] knows no increase or decrease in ordinary people, the…

In the first part, “[suchness’s] own essence and characteristics” takes up greatness in essence and greatness in characteristics together. †

own essence and characteristics · 自體相 zì tǐ xiàng · BDK p. 44 [The essence of suchness] · Wŏnhyo construes 自體相 as introducing 體 and 相 together.
1. Greatness in essence
BDK p. 44 ↗[The essence of suchness] knows no increase or decrease in ordinary people, the…

Next come the words “in all ordinary beings, up to and including the buddhas, it neither increases nor decreases and ultimately abides.” This explains greatness in essence. As the earlier section establishing the meaning puts it, “First, greatness in essence, because suchness is equal in all dharmas and neither increases nor decreases.” †

1. The meaning of “great”

BDK p. 44 ↗[The essence of suchness] knows no increase or decrease in ordinary people, the…

With the passage beginning “Furthermore, suchness in its own essence,” recall that the exposition proper in the section on revealing the correct meaning has two divisions. The first, the explanation of the heading on the dharma, is now complete. The second begins here, explaining the heading on meaning. Two meanings were set out earlier. The text now takes them in order and explains first the meaning of “great.” This too has two parts. First comes a joint account of greatness in essence and greatness in characteristics. ↓ ↓ Then, beginning with “Furthermore,” it explains greatness in activity.

1. Greatness in essence
BDK p. 44 ↗[The essence of suchness] knows no increase or decrease in ordinary people, the…

“Its own essence and characteristics” introduces the two together. † The root text says that in all beings, up to and including the buddhas, it neither increases nor decreases and always abides. † This explains greatness in essence. The earlier Outline says, “First, greatness in essence, since the suchness of all dharmas is equal and neither increases nor decreases.”

BDK p. 44

The greatness of its characteristics

The selection ends at the foot of p. 44, after the answer to “What does this mean?”

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda
B. The Greatness of the Attributes of Suchness

p. 44 From the beginning, suchness in its nature is fully provided with all excellent qualities; namely, it is endowed with the light of great wisdom, [the qualities of] illuminating the entire universe, of true cognition and mind pure in its self-nature; of eternity, bliss, self, and purity; of refreshing coolness, immutability, and freedom. It is endowed with [these excellent qualities] which outnumber the sands of the Ganges [River], which are not independent of, disjointed from, or different from [the essence of suchness], and which are suprarational [attributes of] Buddhahood. Since it is endowed completely with all these, and is not lacking anything, it is called the tathāgatagarbha [when latent] and also the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.

p. 44 Question: It was explained before that the essence of suchness is undifferentiated and devoid of all characteristics. Why is it, then, that you have described its essence as having these various excellent qualities?

p. 44 Answer: Though it has, in reality, all these excellent qualities, it does not have any characteristics of differentiation; it retains its identity and is of one flavor; suchness is solely one.

p. 44 Question: What does this mean? Answer: Since it is devoid of individuation,⁕ it is free from the characteristics of individuation; thus, it is one without any second.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. Greatness in characteristics
BDK p. 44 ↗From the beginning, suchness in its nature is fully provided with all excellent qualities;

Next, “from the outset its nature is itself replete,” and what follows, explains greatness in characteristics. As stated above, “Second, greatness in characteristics, because the tathāgatagarbha is replete with uncontaminated virtues intrinsic to its nature.” † The text has two parts. The first directly sets forth the characteristics of its intrinsic virtues. The second uses an exchange of questions and answers to clarify why this can be said. ↓

2. Why differences in virtue can be spoken of
BDK p. 44 ↗Question: It was explained before that the essence of suchness is undifferentiated and…

The point of the question is clear. The answer first replies in general and then explains in detail. In the detailed explanation it first shows in what sense differences are nondual. It then shows in what sense the nondual admits of differences.

Sources and editorial choices

Base text: Yoshito S. Hakeda, The Awakening of Faith, BDK English Tripiṭaka 63-IV (2005, English translation © 1967 Columbia University Press). The page numbers, wording, and bracketed expansions are Hakeda’s. This collation includes the translated treatise. His separate translator’s notes can be read in the source PDF. Chinese treatise · T1666

The Commentary and Separate Notes are translated from their respective Chinese texts. The Chinese attached to each clause follows the work being translated, including its quotations. The reader uses modern Mandarin citation tones, one syllable per character. Sanskrit glosses give conventional correspondences. They do not imply a surviving Sanskrit original for the treatise.

The section on the two hindrances and the opening account of the coarse characteristic share their translations and anchors with the pp. 11–33 reader. The new material continues with the subtle characteristic and follows the treatise through 是故無二 at the foot of p. 44. Editorial notes flag places where Wŏnhyo’s quoted Chinese or his reading differs from Hakeda’s.
